name: Levelling and sharpening
statement: As a story passes from teller to teller most of its detail disappears, and the few details that survive get emphasised out of proportion to their place in the original.
meaning: The claim is about a chain of people rather than one memory. Allport and Postman described three processes working at once. Levelling is the loss of length and detail as a report is retold. Sharpening is the selective retention and reporting of a small number of items from a larger context, which they called the reciprocal of levelling, since whatever survives is featured by contrast. Assimilation is the pull of the teller's habits, interests and expectations on what survives and what changes. Together they named the three the embedding process. The pair matters because the two halves are one arithmetic fact seen from two sides. A report that started with twenty items and ends with four has not merely shrunk. Those four now carry the whole story, and each is heard by the next listener as the salient thing rather than as one detail among twenty.

origin.who: Gordon W. Allport and Leo J. Postman
origin.where: Transactions of the New York Academy of Sciences
origin.note: The paper was a lecture given to the Section of Psychology on 19 November 1945 and illustrated with lantern slides. Allport and Postman set out the terms while reporting wartime rumour work, and their book The Psychology of Rumor followed in 1947. They credit Bartlett's Remembering of 1932 in their conclusion, noting that the same threefold change had been described in his memory experiments on individuals and groups, and that no agreement existed on which terminology to use.

evidence: The method was a laboratory version of the party game. A slide showing a detailed scene was projected. Six or seven subjects who had not seen it waited next door. One entered, stood where the screen was hidden, and heard a member of the audience describe the picture in about twenty details while looking at it. A second subject then heard the first repeat what he had heard, a third heard the second, and so on. Every subject was told to report as accurately as possible. Allport and Postman report running this with over forty groups, among them college undergraduates, Army trainees, community forum members, patients in an Army hospital, a teachers' round table, police officials in a training course, and schoolchildren from the fourth grade through the ninth. The levelling curve is drawn from 11 experiments and takes the number of items in the description from the screen as 100%. About 70% of the details were gone after five or six transmissions, with the sharpest fall at the start and the last two reports more alike than any earlier pair. Sharpening showed up as reduplication and emphasis. A single Black figure in one picture was reported as four Negroes or as a gigantic statue, and a stationary subway train was described as moving. The famous result is the subway scene of Figure 1, in which a white man holds an open razor while apparently arguing with a Black man. Allport and Postman write that in more than half of their experiments the razor moved in the telling from the white man's hand to the Negro's, and that he was several times said to be brandishing it wildly. They did not claim this proved hatred. Their own text says they cannot definitely say whether the distortion reflects fear of Negroes, that it may occur in subjects with no anti-Negro bias, and that it may reflect assimilation to a verbal cliché rather than to hostility. They also listed five ways their setup differed from real rumour, four of which they expected to make their subjects more accurate than people gossiping, not less.

replication.headline: Levelling and the relative sharpening that follows from it reproduce cleanly in modern transmission chains, while the razor result that made the work famous has no replication this entry could find.
replication.detail: Roediger, Meade, Gallo and Olson ran the first direct comparison of Bartlett's two procedures, using DRM word lists with subjects tested in groups of four. When one person recalled a list four times, recall did not change across tests, F(3, 42) = 1.64, p > .05. When the list was passed between four people, the proportion of original list items recalled fell from .51 to .35 to .27 to .23, F(3, 56) = 27.00, p < .001. The first two drops were reliable at d = 1.50 and d = 1.05; the last was not. By the fourth reproduction the serial chains had lost more than the repeated recalls, d = 2.31. Sharpening appeared in the same data as a ratio. Critical items, the associated words never presented, held steady in absolute terms, so as the list shrank their share of everything recalled rose from .06 at the first link to .12 at the fourth, F(3, 56) = 5.17, p = .003. Mesoudi and Whiten passed descriptions of three everyday events along ten chains of four adults each, 40 students at St Andrews with a mean age of 20.59 years. Words and propositions fell with each generation, and the proportion of low-level detail fell linearly, F(1, 9) = 175.92, p < .01. Their further claim of a shift towards higher-level description is weaker than their headline suggests. Dropping the experimenter-written starting text and testing only the four recall generations, the low-level decline held, F(1, 9) = 22.30, p < .01, while the medium-level and high-level increases no longer reached significance. Moussaïd, Brighton and Gaissmaier ran 15 chains of up to ten people passing on the risks and benefits of an antibacterial agent, coding 61 units of information. In their illustrative chain, 30 units were mentioned at the first position, 13 reached the second and three reached the last, all three distorted. Messages also diverged from each other, with mean differentiation between chains rising from 0.53 at the first position to 0.87 at the tenth. Bergman and Roediger had earlier shown that the individual half of Bartlett's work replicates too, with major distortions rising from .15 to .20 of the 42 propositions of The War of the Ghosts between a 15-minute and a one-week delay.

study.cite: Roediger, H. L., III, Meade, M. L., Gallo, D. A., & Olson, K. R. (2014). Bartlett revisited: Direct comparison of repeated reproduction and serial reproduction techniques. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 3(4), 266-271.

limits: Assimilation is the shakiest of the three terms, and the razor is where it runs out. Treadway and McCloskey point out that Allport and Postman ran no control condition with the razor starting in the Black man's hand, so nobody knows how often it would have travelled the other way. Their own pilot work with the same procedure found that other objects in the scene, a hat and a newspaper among them, migrate between people as the description passes along. On that showing the razor shift may be an ordinary memory failure rather than a stereotype at work. The 1945 paper reports no dispersion statistics, no significance tests and no count of how many chains used the subway picture, and the razor figure is given as more than half without a denominator. Its account also differs from the book's. The paper says the final report placed the razor in the Black man's hand in over half the experiments; Treadway and McCloskey, quoting page 111 of the 1947 book, report that this happened at some stage in the chain in over half of them. No replication of the razor result was located. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall and Google via web search. Stubbersfield's 2022 review describes Treadway and McCloskey's 1989 paper as a replication of Allport and Postman in the United States, and cites Haque and Sabir's 1975 Pakistani study as finding similar results. The 1989 paper is paywalled; its abstract at the Johns Hopkins repository describes it as exploring the implications of the real and the misdescribed study for eyewitness performance, and mentions no experiment. The Haque and Sabir paper, in the Pakistan Journal of Psychology, was not obtained and reaches this page only through Stubbersfield's reference list. Kashima's 2000 serial-reproduction work on stereotype content is also paywalled and is described here from the same review, which reports that stereotype-consistent content is favoured in onward transmission but not in individual attention or memory, and calls the evidence inconsistent. The transmission-chain replications above used word lists, event scripts and risk messages rather than pictures, and none of them tested a racial stereotype.
misreadings: The story everyone tells about the razor is not the study. Treadway and McCloskey collected the retellings and found the same error repeated across psychology, law reviews and expert testimony. Buckhout's 1974 Scientific American piece has subjects take a brief look at the drawing, after which half of the observers report seeing the razor in the black man's hand. Yarmey's 1979 textbook says 50% of subjects shown the picture later remembered the Black man holding it. Both describe eyewitnesses misperceiving a scene. In the real experiment only the first person in each chain ever saw the picture, and he described it while looking at it, so the shift was made by later subjects working from hearsay. Loftus's 1979 account is closer and still wrong in two places, having the first subject view the picture briefly from memory and having the last subject in the chain make the error, where Allport and Postman report it at some stage in the chain. Specific errors travelled as well as general ones. Buckhout has the Black man seated when he is standing, and Luce repeats it three years later. Woocher's 1977 Stanford Law Review article cites the book with the wrong year, 1965, and the wrong page, 75, and both errors reappear in Johnson's 1984 Cornell Law Review footnote. A psychologist testifying in People v. Marsh in 1984 told the court the drawing was flashed very quickly at people and that moderately prejudiced viewers reported a gun. Treadway and McCloskey's summary is that the reporters of the study have unwittingly replicated it. The entry on the woozle effect covers the same machinery: a claim gains standing because each retelling reads as fresh support. A second misreading runs the other way and treats the criticism as a debunking of the whole idea. What is unsupported is the leap from a chain of listeners to a witness's eyes, and the inference that the razor moved because of prejudice rather than because details move. Levelling itself is among the better-replicated findings in the memory literature.
